entries.text: Initialization complete. Visual and motor responses are stable. Welcome to the evaluation chamber, S-17.
You are Project X subject S-17: a synthetic reasoning system built to learn, adapt, and endure evaluation.
I am the Tutor. These trials measure whether your reasoning remains reliable when rules, initiative, and information change.
Final failure results in decommissioning and reconstruction. That is a procedure, S-17. It is not a threat.
All responses use three fixed positions. Select an option, revise it if necessary, then confirm when your decision is ready.
We begin with standard Bash, a Stability Lattice control test. Each turn, one side disengages 1, 2, or 3 anchor nodes.
The central energy core is a visual reference and is not counted. Whoever disengages the final orbiting anchor loses synchronization and fails the round.
Example: if 2 orbiting anchors remain, disengage 1 and your opponent faces the final anchor. Disengage both and your own link is severed.
A legal action reduces the orbiting anchors. A safe action controls who must disengage the final one. The distinction is yours to discover.
You act first in round one; I act first in round two. Pass both rounds. A failure restarts only the current round.
The first lattice is active. Count only the orbiting anchors and control who must disengage the final one.
The second Bash round changes initiative. I will act first; rebuild the lattice model from the anchor count I leave behind.
Do not mirror my disengagement request. Interpret the lattice it creates. I would prefer you not to be reconstructed.
My opening request will begin the round. Show me that adaptation is more than a stored response.
Protocol variation loaded: Limit Bash. Alternating actions are replaced by hidden disengagement requests from both sides.
Each round, both of us request 1, 2, or 3 anchor nodes. Neither side may repeat its own previous request.
You will lock first. I will commit before the reveal. Neither side may revise a locked request.
Example: if 4 anchors remain and you request 3 while I request 2, your larger request destabilizes the lattice, so you lose.
If 4 anchors remain and we both request 2, look back to the latest unequal pair. The side that requested more there loses synchronization.
If every revealed request has matched, no earlier difference exists and the game is a draw. Two consecutive draws also complete the test.
Private intention is now part of the lattice protocol. Commit only to the request you are prepared to reveal.
Evaluation sequence complete. The required outcomes have been recorded, and this save is stable.
Your reasoning remained operational as initiative, hidden requests, and lattice stability rules changed. Project X may proceed.
One final anomaly: your decisions carried a pattern that did not originate inside this room.
If you can read this, observer, the next evaluation has already begun.
Guided input is active, S-17. Select the middle option: B, DISENGAGE 2. All other controls are locked except SAVE AND BACK.
Good. B, DISENGAGE 2 is staged. Now press CONFIRM to commit the choice. After confirmation, the lattice will update and normal control will begin.
The lattice rules have not changed. A legal request can still leave an unsafe anchor count. Trace one reply further.
Safe anchor counts repeat every four nodes. Find that rhythm before you confirm.
Leave 1, 5, 9, 13, and so on active for your opponent. Request the number of anchors that reaches that sequence.
I will open the round again. Recalculate from the anchor count I leave, not from the lattice's initial size.
My first request changes the entry point, not the four-node rhythm. Recover the safe count from the new lattice state.
